summary: This informational document explains why many Internet applications need object-based security mechanisms. The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) has long offered a binary format based on ASN.1. It sets out use cases and requirements for a JSON-based approach, JOSE.

plainLanguage.summary: Many programs need to lock and sign packages of data. This lists why and what is needed for a version that uses JSON.

subtitle: Why JSON-based object security matters for web and cloud applications.

tldr.problem: Many Internet applications need to protect data with cryptographic security at the object level, not just at the transport or network layer. For decades, binary formats like ASN.1 have been used, but modern applications rely on text-based formats like JSON, which lack robust security tools.
tldr.mechanism: This document outlines use cases and requirements for JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE), a JSON-based format for signed and encrypted objects, symmetric and asymmetric keys, and cryptographic algorithms.
tldr.outcome: JOSE specifications (JWS, JWE, JWK, JWA) were developed by the IETF to provide developers with simple, JSON-native security mechanisms for OAuth, OpenID Connect, XMPP, alerts, and constrained devices.

today: RFC 7165 is an Informational document from April 2014. The JOSE specifications it motivated (JWS, JWE, JWK, JWA) became foundational to modern Internet security. OAuth 2.0 access tokens are almost universally issued as JWTs. OpenID Connect relies on JOSE for identity tokens and request objects. XMPP and IoT platforms use JOSE for encryption. Browser APIs expose JWK format. As of 2024, JOSE is ubiquitous in web and cloud application security.

sections.title: Why Object-Based Security
sections.content:
Applications often cannot rely on transport-layer security alone (like TLS), because data must be protected even when it passes through untrusted intermediaries. Email is the classic example: a message in transit passes through multiple Mail Transfer Agents (MTAs) before reaching its destination. Even though each hop may use TLS, the intermediaries themselves can still read and modify the message. To protect against intermediaries, applications need object-based security: the data itself is wrapped in a cryptographic envelope that proves its origin and protects its content, and untrusted entities can handle it safely.

For decades, Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), defined in ASN.1 and encoded in binary, has served this role. However, modern applications have grown skilled at handling text-based formats like JSON and XML, but often lack tools for ASN.1. Developers faced a choice: either implement complex ASN.1 processing, or forgo object-based security. To make object security accessible to modern developers, the IETF chartered the JOSE working group to build secure object formats based on JSON.
sections.plainLanguage: When mail passes through a post office, the postmaster could read it. A sealed letter, signed by the sender, proves it is real and nobody opened it. Modern computers speak JSON fluently but struggle with old math notation. This RFC asks: what does JSON security need to do?

sections.title: The JOSE Suite and Its Components
sections.content:
JOSE comprises four specifications that work together:

JSON Web Signature (JWS) provides integrity protection and data origin authentication using either symmetric keys (MACs) or asymmetric keys (digital signatures). A JWS object wraps a payload (the actual data) with a signature header that proves the data has not been tampered with and came from a known sender.

JSON Web Encryption (JWE) provides confidentiality by encrypting a payload. It supports both symmetric and asymmetric encryption and allows wrapped keys to be included in the object—encrypted copies of the encryption key, one per recipient in a multi-recipient scenario.

JSON Web Key (JWK) defines a JSON format for cryptographic keys—public keys, private keys (wrapped for safe transmission), and symmetric keys, along with metadata such as the key's algorithm and permitted uses.

JSON Web Algorithms (JWA) specifies which cryptographic algorithms are allowed and how to apply them. This ensures all implementations use algorithms the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: JWS is a signature that proves a message came from someone. JWE is a lock that hides the message. JWK is a format for storing keys. JWA lists which math tricks are allowed and how to use them.

sections.title: Where JOSE Is Needed
sections.content: The RFC details eight major use cases. Security tokens (used by OAuth, OpenID Connect, and SAML) embed claims about a user or resource in a signed or encrypted JSON object. OAuth uses JOSE to protect access tokens as they move from an authorization server to a resource server via a resource owner, ensuring the server can verify the token's origin and integrity. OpenID Connect uses JOSE tokens for identity and for signing other protocol messages. XMPP (instant messaging) uses JOSE for end-to-end encryption, separating the encryption of a message (sent once to all recipients) from wrapping the encryption key separately for each recipient. ALTO (traffic optimization) signs large JSON network-topology objects that flow through intermediaries. Emergency alerts require multiple signatures from different authorities along the distribution chain (originator, gateway, network operator, device). Web Cryptography APIs in browsers need JWK to export and import keys safely. Constrained devices (IoT, sensors) need compact, minimal-overhead JOSE objects for very small payloads where encryption overhead would be prohibitive.
sections.plainLanguage: Tokens prove who you are. OAuth hands out permission slips. XMPP sends secret messages. ALTO signs big network maps. Alerts come through many stops. Browsers manage keys. Tiny sensors send a byte that must be locked.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
sections.content:
From these use cases, the RFC derives functional requirements. JOSE must support signing and encryption using both symmetric and asymmetric keys—MACs for shared-secret scenarios, digital signatures when only public keys are known. It must define both JSON and compact URL-safe serializations: JSON serialization for readability and extensibility, compact serialization (a dotted base64url string) for scenarios with space constraints such as HTTP query parameters.

Cryptographic parameters must be carried in the object itself, not pre-negotiated, so an implementation can recognize whether it has the key needed to process an object. Wrapped keys must be separable from the encrypted payload, so multiple recipients can share the same ciphertext and only the wrapped key varies per recipient. Attributes of keys must be bound to wrapped keys cryptographically, so restrictions on how a key can be used are protected along with the key itself. And the format must not impose more overhead than necessary, especially when protecting large payloads.
sections.plainLanguage: It must work with shared secrets and public keys. It must fit in a URL and be human-readable. It must say what math it uses. Multiple people can unlock the same box. Key rules must be locked with the key. It must not balloon the message size.

sections.title: Security and Cryptographic Considerations
sections.content:
JOSE must enforce security best practices. Long-lived symmetric keys should not be used directly for encryption or authentication; instead, they should wrap per-message session keys. Cryptographic algorithms must be used in modes and combinations approved by major standards bodies, so developers do not accidentally combine weak algorithms or use them incorrectly. Operation without pre-negotiation is required—any two parties with a key can communicate without pre-arranging parameters—but implementations must recognize when they lack the key and fail cleanly rather than silently proceeding with wrong keys.

A critical challenge is that JSON lacks a canonical form: two JSON objects can represent identical data but differ in whitespace, key ordering, or numeric representation. This complicates signature verification: an attacker might manipulate the JSON representation so the signature still validates but the data is interpreted differently by downstream applications. To avoid this, JOSE avoids canonicalization and instead encodes the signed data in base64url form, preserving the exact bytes that were signed.
sections.plainLanguage: Short keys should not be used directly; wrap them first. Use math tricks that experts trust. Know when you do not have the right key. JSON can be written many ways, so lock the exact bytes instead of the meaning.

sections.title: Why JOSE Succeeded
sections.content: JOSE succeeded where earlier attempts at XML-based security (XML Signatures, XML Encryption) had struggled, because JSON is simpler than XML, and JOSE avoids complex canonicalization. The working group focused on simplicity and developer accessibility: the formats are compact, the algorithms are straightforward, and the JSON serialization is readable. This low barrier to entry drove rapid adoption in OAuth, OpenID Connect, and dozens of other applications. By meeting the specific needs of modern, text-based applications while maintaining cryptographic rigor, JOSE became a foundational building block for Internet application security.
sections.plainLanguage: JOSE is simpler and more popular than older ways because JSON is easier than the old notation, and JOSE does not require confusing tricks. Developers love it and use it everywhere.
